transcript:
Meeting header: 2028-09-12 15:00 UTC | Duration 62m | Attendees: Jordan Ellis (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Ava Park (Helios CTO), Marco Ruiz (Helios ML), Sofia Chen (Helios Infra)

[00:00] Jordan Ellis: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, quick roll call and then we'd like to surface a crisp POC charter for latency and throughput SLOs — ttft versus tpot, measurement plan, and timeline.
[00:18] Ava Park: thanks Jordan, yes we want something pragmatic — we run customer-facing chat and some document-summarization endpoints. Main asks: keep latency tight for UI interactions and make cost predictable.
[00:32] Marco Ruiz: hi all, quick context: our traffic is spiky, peak windows at 9am and 7pm UTC; median prompt length 120 tokens, but tail at 900 tokens. We care about both first-response snappy experience and overall per-request cost.
[00:49] Maya Singh: great, helps. two quick defs so we align: TTFT = time-to-first-token, the latency the user notices when typing start-of-response. TPOT we use as total-per-token throughput metric — effectively average per-token processing latency that scales with sequence length.
[01:10] Sofia Chen: can you clarify how you choose which metric to prioritize? we might accept slightly higher TTFT in exchange for lower cost on long requests — do you typically see clear tradeoffs?
[01:24] Jordan Ellis: yes exactly, it's a tradeoff. For chat UI TTFT usually dominates UX, so we set aggressive p95 targets there; for batch summarization TPOT (per-token) drives cost and tail latency. In pilots we often test both and set guardrails: e.g., TTFT p95 target and TPOT p95 per-token target with a p99 watch.
[01:44] Marco Ruiz: what are typical numbers you recommend? our current baseline on-cloud is p95 TTFT ~270ms and p99 ~1.2s which feels too high for interactive.
[01:56] Maya Singh: ok that's useful. For interactive chat we usually aim for TTFT p95 < 200ms and p99 < 500-600ms for a premium tier. For cost-optimized tiers we set TTFT p95 < 350ms and p99 < 1s. For TPOT we express as ms/token: p95 ~30-50ms/token and p99 <120ms/token for medium models; big models will be higher. But those are starting points, we'll tune to your traffic.
[02:26] Ava Park: that p99 spread is big though — how do you measure p99 reliably? we have only 10-20% of requests in the tail.
[02:36] Maya Singh: measurement plan: phase 1 run synthetic and replayed traffic to ensure sample sizes; phase 2, run a 48-72 hour production shadow with sampled logging capturing detailed timing (TTFT, last-token, per-token breakdown). We'll use percentile estimation with bootstrapping to stabilize p99. We also recommend isolating warm/cold start effects by keeping a warm cache or running warmup passes.
[03:02] Marco Ruiz: replay — would you need full request body? we can't share PHI — will need to scrub.
[03:09] Jordan Ellis: absolutely, scrubbed/anonymized logs are fine. we just need sequence length, tokenization counts, timestamps and a safe ID for correlating. If there are regulatory constraints we can run the benchmark in your VPC/private deployment.
[03:25] Sofia Chen: that's good. question on infrastructure: do you run quantized model variants and fallback policies in the same POC? we want to see impact of int8 quant vs fp16 on both TTFT and TPOT.
[03:37] Maya Singh: yes, common pattern: we propose running 2 variants in the pilot — a performance-optimized (fp16) and a cost-optimized (int8/quant) variant. routing policies can send interactive traffic to perf variant and long jobs to cost variant. For measurement we'll record both per-variant metrics and an overall service-level aggregation.
[03:58] Ava Park: can you give an example acceptance criteria (we need to put in the procurement doc)?
[04:04] Jordan Ellis: example acceptance criteria: During a 48-hour pilot window with production-like traffic (sampled from your scrubbed logs), the perf variant must achieve TTFT p95 <= 200ms and TTFT p99 <= 600ms for interactive route; the cost variant must show TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token and end-to-end success rate > 99.5%. We'll also include a fallback check — under 2 minute sustained load spike, fallback to a lower-cost region without more than 3% error increase.
[04:34] Marco Ruiz: metrics we care about also include tokens/sec throughput, GPU utilization, and RU (request units) cost estimates.
[04:41] Maya Singh: we will instrument token counters, GPU and inference host metrics, and compute unit costs. Redwood Console will provide token-level cost breakdown per route so you can map to product economics.
[04:55] Jordan Ellis: quick qualification — what's your timeline and decision criteria?
[05:00] Ava Park: target pilot in the next 2 weeks ideally, procurement sign-off by end of month. success for us is both meeting the TTFT targets on the interactive route and having a predictable cost model for 3 months of expected usage.
[05:12] Sofia Chen: tech constraints: Helios uses VPC-first approach; any customer data must remain in our VPC during the pilot. we prefer Redwood Private but can do Dedicated if needed.
[05:23] Jordan Ellis: understood. for VPC/on-prem we can offer a private agent to run the benchmark inside your network; it will still report aggregated metrics to Redwood Console but no payload leaves your VPC. We'll flag a security review.
[05:36] Ava Park: good. about measurement windows — you mentioned warmup earlier, what do you recommend for warmup length and sample rates?
[05:44] Maya Singh: warmup: 10-15 minutes of ramping traffic for GPU kernels and KV cache population; longer if you have cold models. For p99 stability we'll want 48-72 hours of sampling at full traffic or a carefully replayed 10-20x synthetic to generate enough tails. We'll also run focused microbenchmarks (single-client, high-QPS) to isolate kernel bottlenecks.
[06:09] Marco Ruiz: microbenchmarks — do you provide the harness?
[06:12] Jordan Ellis: yes, Maya has a Jupyter perf-run notebook and a containerized harness that runs both single-shot and ramp tests. We'll share that as part of the runbook.
[06:22] Maya Singh: note, harness supports sending both streaming and non-streaming requests so we can measure TTFT (streaming) vs full-response (non-streaming) differences. We'll also capture KV cache hit rates which matter for conversational context.
[06:36] Sofia Chen: interesting — for chat we use streaming to show partial answers in the UI, so TTFT is essential. can you break down how much of TTFT is network vs model vs runtime?
[06:47] Maya Singh: we'll produce a waterfall: client-to-edge network, edge-to-inference, runtime scheduling, kernel execution, and token serialization. With traces we typically see ~20-40% network, ~30-40% runtime scheduling and kernel, rest serialization—varies based on region and model.
[07:06] Ava Park: assume we meet p95 but p99 misses — what remediation?
[07:11] Jordan Ellis: standard playbook: analyze traces to find correlation (long prompts, cache misses, cold starts), tune batch sizes, warmup, and possibly fall back to smaller model variant for the long-tail. We can also put an SLO banding where 95% production traffic hits strict SLO and 1% allowed to be slower with an agreed action plan.
[07:32] Marco Ruiz: sample sizes again — if we only run 24 hours we might not get stable p99 — you insist on 48-72. is there a quicker way?
[07:40] Maya Singh: you can augment with synthetic tails — run synthetic long-tail requests at controlled rates to produce p99 behavior faster. But we prefer real-traffic replay for fidelity.
[07:51] Ava Park: cost of pilot — will you provide trial credits or is cost significant?
[07:55] Jordan Ellis: Redwood usually provides pilot credits for the hosted side; for Dedicated/Private there might be some infra cost. We can estimate during next step once we lock the workload profile.
[08:06] Sofia Chen: one operational ask — can we collect per-request trace IDs and map them back to our logs?
[08:11] Maya Singh: yes we support correlation IDs, and we'll provide a mapping in the runbook. All telemetry will be TTL-limited and scrubbable.
[08:18] Jordan Ellis: ok let's sketch the POC plan and timeline now. High-level phases: discovery & data handoff (3 business days), baseline microbenchmarks (2 days), pilot execution (48-72h), analysis & tuning (3 business days), handoff & runbook (2 days). So ~2 weeks from start to final report.
[08:40] Ava Park: sounds reasonable. for discovery we'll need a security questionnaire answered and an NDA signed.
[08:46] Jordan Ellis: we'll attach the security pack and standard pilot NDA in email.
[08:50] Marco Ruiz: for the baseline configs — what GPUs and instance types will you use? we need the perf numbers to map to our capacity planning.
[08:58] Maya Singh: by default perf variant uses A5000-class or equivalent (we'll specify exact GPU family in the runbook) and cost variant uses quantized instances on A100-like or mixed. We'll provide per-model throughput numbers and a sizing table (qps per GPU at 95% utilization) in the final report.
[09:16] Ava Park: let's put concrete SLOs in the charter: interactive route TTFT p95 <= 200ms, p99 <= 600ms; batch summarization TPOT p95 <= 60ms/token, p99 <= 150ms/token; error rate < 0.5%; cost variance <= 15% of estimates during pilot.
[09:36] Jordan Ellis: noted, we'll include that as a draft acceptance matrix in the runbook.
[09:41] Sofia Chen: final Q: can you simulate multi-region failover so we can validate graceful degradation?
[09:47] Maya Singh: yes we can run an az/region failover test during the pilot with controlled traffic; we'll capture failover latency and error delta.
[09:56] Jordan Ellis: ok quick recap of next steps — action items we captured in the call notes. we'll share the perf harness, the security pack, and a concrete pilot calendar. Also we'll ask Helios to provide scrubbed traffic and confirm VPC or Dedicated preference.
[10:14] Ava Park: we'll aim to get the logs and sign off NDA by 2028-09-16 and hope to start the week of 2028-09-25.
[10:21] Jordan Ellis: perfect — thanks everyone. any last questions?
[10:24] Marco Ruiz: none from me, thanks.
[10:26] Sofia Chen: none, thanks.
[10:28] Jordan Ellis: thanks all — chat after for scheduling.

Summary (auto): POC scoping focused on defining TTFT vs TPOT SLOs, measurement plan and pilot timeline. Agreed to run two model variants (perf & cost), collect scrubbed traffic, run 48-72h pilot with warmup and microbenchmarks, and measure TTFT p95/p99 and TPOT ms/token p95/p99. Security and data residency are gating items; Redwood to provide runbook, harness, and security pack.

Links shared during call: Perf harness (drive link), Redwood POC runbook (redwood.com/poc-runbook), security pack (redwood.com/security/note), sample acceptance matrix (attached in follow-up).

End of transcript.
